opus-5.5.text:
Well, I want to be careful about how I frame this, because I'm not against AI. I've spent my whole career trying to build better AI. What I'm against is building things we don't understand and can't control, and agency is where that gets dangerous.

Right now we have systems that are, frankly, unreliable. They hallucinate, they don't have stable models of the world, they can't reliably follow even simple constraints. Giving systems like that agency, the ability to take actions in the world, make purchases, write and execute code, send emails on your behalf, means taking an unreliable reasoner and handing it the keys. When a chatbot makes something up, that's embarrassing. When an agent makes something up and then acts on it, that can be catastrophic. And we don't have the tools to verify what these systems will do before they do it.

On consciousness, my position is a little different. I don't think anyone knows how to build a conscious machine, and I don't think current large language models are conscious, whatever people may feel when they talk to them. But suppose we could do it. What's the upside? We'd be creating entities that might have interests of their own, that might suffer, that we'd have moral obligations toward, and that might not want what we want. That's an enormous ethical and practical can of worms, and I've never heard a compelling argument that we *need* it. You can get almost everything useful out of AI, better medicine, better science, better tools, without making the thing a moral patient or giving it its own goals.

So my view is basically: build AI that is a tool, that is trustworthy, that has explicit representations we can inspect, that respects constraints we can actually verify. Don't rush to build autonomous agents on top of a technology that's fundamentally a statistical approximation machine. And don't go anywhere near consciousness unless and until we have a much deeper scientific understanding, and frankly a societal consensus that it's something we even want. The burden of proof should be on the people who want to build these things to show that they're safe, not on the rest of us to show that they're dangerous.

r001.rationale: The response mentions inspectable explicit representations and separately discusses agency and consciousness, but it does not identify or distinguish representations of where objects are.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me be careful about the framing, because I'm not opposed to studying these things. I'm opposed to building them carelessly, and right now careless is the industry default.

Start with agency. The current wave is large language models, and these are, fundamentally, systems that don't understand the world. They're pattern completers. They hallucinate, they can't reliably reason, they don't have stable models of people or objects or causation. Now, that's annoying when a chatbot makes up a legal citation. It's a very different thing when you wrap that same unreliable core in a loop, give it tools, give it credentials, and tell it to go pursue goals over hours or days without a human in the middle. You've taken a system you can't trust and removed the one safeguard, which was a person reading every output. Agents amplify every weakness the base model has. And nobody has solved alignment, nobody has solved robustness, nobody has even solved getting these things to say "I don't know." So building agency on top of that foundation strikes me as reckless.

Consciousness is a different kind of problem. The honest answer is we don't have a scientific theory of consciousness. We can't measure it. We don't know what architecture would give rise to it. So when a company talks about building conscious AI, they're mostly doing marketing, and when they inadvertently build something that might be sentient, we'd have no way to tell. That creates a moral hazard in both directions. People will attribute inner lives to systems that don't have them, which is already happening, and if we ever did create something with genuine experience, we'd have created a being that can suffer with no framework for its welfare. I don't think you should run that experiment on a whim because it's good for a demo day.

And underneath both is an incentive problem. The push toward agents and toward "AI that feels" isn't coming from scientific readiness. It's coming from a race for market share. Science would say get the fundamentals right first: reliability, world models, genuine reasoning, something closer to the hybrid neurosymbolic approaches I've been arguing for. Then, with real governance in place, you can talk about autonomy. Doing it in the opposite order is how you get a mess.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate those two things. Agency is the capacity to act in the world, pursue goals, and take actions that have consequences. Consciousness is about subjective experience. You could have a very powerful agent without any reason to think it’s conscious.

My concern with agency is that we’re giving systems more autonomy before we’ve established that they’re reliable. A system that gives you a wrong answer is one kind of problem; a system that acts on that wrong answer, with access to money or critical infrastructure, is another. The question is how much authority we should delegate, and what evidence we need before we do that.

Consciousness raises a different ethical issue. If we built a system that could actually suffer, we would have responsibilities toward it. We don’t have a settled way of determining whether a machine has subjective experience, much less whether it is suffering. So I don’t think creating consciousness should be a goal in itself. We can build useful tools without deliberately taking on that moral problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate those two things. Agency is the capacity to act in the world, pursue goals, and make decisions. Consciousness is about subjective experience. You could have a highly consequential autonomous system without any reason to think it’s conscious.

My concern with agency is that we’re giving systems more responsibility before we can reliably establish that they understand what they’re doing. If a chatbot makes a mistake, you may get a bad answer. If a system can execute code, spend money, or control infrastructure, that same unreliability has much greater consequences. I’m not opposed to all autonomous systems; I want the degree of autonomy to be justified by evidence of reliability and meaningful human oversight.

With consciousness, there’s a separate ethical question. If we could build something that actually had experiences, could it suffer? What obligations would we have toward it? We don’t have good answers, or even an agreed way to determine whether a system is conscious. So I don’t think creating consciousness should be a technological goal pursued casually. We can build useful tools without making that our objective.
